column1: In the deletion rule on slide 7, a node with two children is replaced by its in-order ____, which is the smallest key in its right subtree.
column2:
successor
Slide 7 names the in-order successor as the smallest key in the right subtree, and notes the in-order predecessor — the largest key in the left subtree — works too.

column1: In a binary min-heap stored in an array with index 0 as the root, the parent of the node at index i is at index ____.
column2:
Math.floor((i - 1) / 2) (also: Math.floor((i-1)/2), floor((i - 1) / 2), floor((i-1)/2), ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋, ⌊(i-1)/2⌋)
Slide 5 gives the parent of index i as floor((i - 1) / 2); the floor is what makes it correct for even indices, where the division does not come out whole (index 6: (6 − 1) / 2 = 2.5, floor 2).

column1: Explain what primary clustering is and why linear probing produces it. Then state one way double hashing reduces it.
column2:
Primary clustering is the growth of contiguous runs of occupied slots. Linear probing causes it because every key that hashes into a run probes forward one slot at a time and lands at the end of that run, lengthening it, so the run attracts still more keys. Double hashing reduces it by making the step size depend on the key, so two keys that collide at the same slot probe different sequences instead of both walking the same consecutive slots.
Occupied runs grow because linear probing walks consecutive slots, and slide 11 shows this with 89 in slot 9, 49 in slot 0, 58 in slot 1 and 69 in slot 2. Double hashing varies the step per key, so colliding keys do not share one probe sequence.

column1:
A hash table uses separate chaining with m = 8 buckets and holds n = 20 entries. A classmate says the table is over-full and must be resized before any more inserts. Which statement is correct?
a) The classmate is right: α = 2.5 exceeds 1, and no hash table may exceed α = 1.
b) The classmate is wrong: with chaining α may exceed 1, and the cost is longer chains and a higher average probe count.
c) The classmate is right: α = 2.5 means 2.5 buckets are already full and the next insert will fail.
d) The classmate is wrong: α measures only the number of empty buckets, which is still 8 − 20.
column2:
The classmate is wrong: with chaining α may exceed 1, and the cost is longer chains and a higher average probe count.
Slide 13 puts the α ≤ 1 limit on open addressing only, because there every entry must occupy a slot in the array. Separate chaining stores entries in lists outside the array, so α can exceed 1; the cost is that the average chain length is α = 20/8 = 2.5, which raises the average search cost even though it stays O(1) average.

column1: Slide 9 inserts 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101 into a chained table with m = 7 and h(k) = k mod 7, adding each new entry at the end of its chain. A search for 57, which is not in the table, compares 57 with every key in its chain. How many key comparisons does it make? Give your answer in comparisons.
column2:
3 comparisons
57 mod 7 = 1, because 57 = 8 × 7 + 1. Bucket 1 holds the chain 50 → 85 → 92, and 57 is not in it, so the search compares 57 with all three keys before it reaches the end of the chain: 3 comparisons.

column1: A BST holds n nodes. State its worst-case height and describe an insertion order that produces it. Explain in two or three sentences why that order is the worst.
column2:
The worst-case height is n - 1 edges, giving a tree that is a single chain. Inserting keys in sorted order, ascending or descending, produces it: in ascending order each new key is larger than every key already present, so every insertion walks right from the root and attaches as the rightmost leaf (descending order mirrors this on the left). The height is then n - 1 because the longest root-to-leaf path visits every node, and search costs O(h) = O(n), no better than a list.
Slide 8: inserting keys in sorted order (1, 2, 3, …) builds a chain of height n − 1, so search, insert and delete all cost O(n) instead of O(log n).

column1: A min-heap is stored in an array with 14 elements, using the slide's 0-based indexing. During one `extract-min`, after the last leaf is moved to the root, how many array elements does the sift-down loop examine in total across all its iterations — counting each child index that is compared against the current node? Give the maximum possible number for a heap of this size, as a whole number. Give your answer in child comparisons.
column2:
6 child comparisons
Sift-down descends at most one level per iteration and the tree of 14 nodes is 3 levels deep below the root, so the loop runs at most 3 times; each iteration inspects a left child and a right child, giving at most 6 child comparisons.

column1: Slide 3 of Lecture 4 lists CPU and job scheduling and Dijkstra's shortest paths as applications of priority queues. Choose one of those two and explain why a binary heap suits it specifically — refer to the operation the application performs most often and the heap's cost for that operation compared with the alternatives on slide 12.
column2:
Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly removes the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, which is exactly extract-min, and relaxes edges, which lowers tentative distances — a decrease-key. A binary heap does both in O(log n), while an unsorted array does extract-min in O(n) and a sorted array does decrease-key in O(n). So the two operations the algorithm repeats most are cheap on a heap and slow on at least one of them on either array.
Slide 12: a binary heap does extract-min and decrease-key in O(log n), while an unsorted array needs O(n) for extract-min and a sorted array O(n) for decrease-key.
